Supply-Resources and Development on the whole the provinces have done much better in that respect than the federal government.
The housing problem resolves itself into two phases. In the first place there is a dire need for houses. The best the hon. member for Spadina could say about the achievements of the government in the matter of housing was that during the past four years they have succeeded in building about 100,000 fewer houses than new Canadian families required. In other words in that four-year period they have dropped back about 100,000 houses, which have been added to that backlog which existed at the end of the war. I do not think the hon. member's figures do justice to the government in that respect. The figures contained in the 1950 report of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are different from those quoted by the hon. member, and indicate that as of the end of 1950 we still needed close to half a million houses. I am prepared to be a little more lenient in this respect than the hon. member for Spadina. I think the very best that can be said of the achievements of the government since 1946 is that they have barely kept up with the need for new houses arising from year to year. We still have just as much of a housing shortage today as we had at the end of the war. That is the first fact.
I was delighted to hear the hon. member for Spadina, in the latter part of his speech which I suggested should go out to his riding, disapprove of the minister's marriage to private enterprise; that he felt there was a place for the government to take action in housing; that there was a place for publicly financed housing, particularly in the low rental group. The truth of the matter is that the provision of low or even moderate rental housing is not a commercial proposition at all with today's building costs. It is impossible for private builders to provide low rental housing, or even moderate rental housing. It is this field in which there is a great need for houses today, and if that need is to be met it must be met by public financing.
The prospect for catching up on that backlog of half a million houses is not very bright. In the 1950 report of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation it is stated on page 6 that residential construction is that part of the construction industry least able to secure building materials in periods of shortage. In numerous places in the report there is the suggestion that the shortage of building materials in 1951 is likely to curtail the building of residential properties. According to that report, the picture is not nearly as bright as
3814	HOUSE OF
Supply-Resources and Development the one painted by the minister this afternoon. Even last year when, according to the minister, there was no shortage to affect housing, and when the department was advancing an additional loan of one-sixth of the basic mortgage, the net increase in houses was 83,000. According to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation report, the net increase in family and non-family households for the same year was 87,000. In other words last year, under those favourable conditions, we fell 4,000 short of keeping up with the new demands created during that year. We added an additional 4,000 to that backlog which had been piling up during the depression and during the war years.
Since that was the best we could do last year, what are the prospects for the coming year when we are faced with a defence program which will have first call upon our materials? It is quite evident that unless some priority is established whereby residential housing may secure building materials, we are going to add still further to that backlog. As a matter of fact, residential housing has never received its fair proportion of the men and materials available. According to the government publication, "Private and Public Investment in Canada in 1947," residential housing got only 34-3 per cent of the total construction expenditures; in 1948, 35 per cent; and in 1949, 34-8 per cent. Then, according to the corporation's report for 1950, the over-all share of men and materials that went into housing construction dropped back about four per cent as compared with 1949. This report indicates that housing construction is not likely to get its fair share of construction materials and labour in a situation such as that which faces us today.
I would suggest that one of the first steps in order to increase or maintain the building program, and to avoid adding still further to that half million shortage, should be a system of priorities for construction materials. I believe that is a must for the government. The second problem so far as housing is concerned is the cost of houses today. It places them beyond the reach of many thousands of our people, beyond their reach either to buy or to rent. I should like to refer to an article in the Economics and Political Science issue of 1949 which is entitled "The Economics of Low Rental Housing." This article is two years old, but the situation has not changed very much. The statement is made that the lowest income group, constituting 20-7 per cent of the population, could not afford to buy a house at all. The next group, 12-7 per cent, could not 

afford to own a house costing more than $3,000 or $4,000. That rules out one-third of our people who could not afford to own a house costing more than $3,000 or $4,000 two years ago, and who certainly could not secure any of the houses which are built at today's prices. There is practically one-third of our population for whom publicly financed houses must be provided if they are to secure houses. The next 20 per cent could not afford one costing more than $4,000 to $5,000. The next 12-1 per cent could not afford one costing more than $5,000 to $6,000. It is therefore quite evident that, at present prices, a large proportion of those who need housing accommodation-those in the lower income brackets -just cannot afford either to buy or to rent houses that are built even with government assistance at today's prices.
On page 11 of the report of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation I find that 4,311 housing units were provided through arrangement with builders and investors under what is called the rental insurance plan.

For what year was that
report?

For the year 1950. The average number of rooms in those 4,311 houses is four. The average, rental is given at $70 a month. That is $70 a month for a four-roomed house. That is the average for 4,311 of these houses built across the country by investors and builders, through arrangements with the government. That price puts those houses beyond the reach of hundreds of thousands of those in the low-wage category.
As was indicated by the hon. member for Spadina, the need for low-rental housing is one of the great needs today. I think, as does the hon. member for Spadina, that the advantage which some of the provinces have already taken of section 35 of the National Housing Act is probably one of the brightest features of that report. In two of those projects at least the rental is based on 20 per cent of the tenant's income, in the case of unheated accommodation, and on 25 per cent of the tenant's income in the homes that were heated. That provides the legislative machinery necessary for solving the housing problem of those in the lower income groups. Certainly the minister should be encouraged to press forward with getting an increase in the number of agreements with the provinces, and in giving the provinces every possible encouragement to provide these low-rental houses on this basis.

Another difficulty in connection with our present housing situation is the matter of financing. When the minister introduced the measure by which an additional one-sixth loan was provided for builders he told us, in his own words, as reported at page 1295 of Hansard of 1949:
We are establishing a pattern for long-term housing development . . .
Four months ago it became evident that the long term was instead a short term of about one year; for although that legislation remains on the statute books, the government has arbitrarily cancelled that feature of the legislation because it became the government's avowed policy to restrict building. I think it was made quite clear that the reason for cancelling this one-sixth loan was for the express purpose of curtailing residential building, in spite of the fact that we still need half a million new houses. It has been indicated by the minister himself and others, as well as in the report of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, that the government was afraid that there would not be sufficient material available to build all the houses that would be started if that one-sixth mortgage loan still remained available.
Apparently the minister believes that if we are to solve the housing problem, we must be prepared to accept a lower standard of housing. I think he told us that if we could reduce by about 15 per cent the standard of housing that the Canadian housewife wants to live in, we would solve a fair part of our housing problem. I doubt if the Canadian people today believe that the only way Canada can work itself out of its present difficulty is by reducing living standards. The other evening the Minister of Finance gave us the same policy: the need for reducing living standards. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that we in Canada-even though, as the minister says, there is a housing shortage in all the countries of the world-have natural resources, in men and material, available for providing our people with houses, without lowering the standard of the houses with which our people should be provided. I suggest that the minister should restore that one-sixth loan in order to enable purchasers to make the necessary down payment on the houses that we are building.
There is another feature of housing financing that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. Since he has raised the interest rate for finance companies the builders tell me-and as a matter of fact two of them told me this only today-that finance 80709-243
7, 1951	3815
Supply-Resources and Development companies are still refusing to advance moneys for building under the National Housing Act; that it is still practically impossible to get those loans; that the 5J per cent which the finance companies would get is still not sufficient to warrant their lending money under the National Housing Act. I should like a statement from the minister on that. I want to assure him that today there are builders whose applications were approved two or three months ago who were rejected because of the interest rate, and are still being rejected. I do not think the answer is a further increase in interest rates to mortgage companies, but I do think that the government has to take some measures. If they cannot get the mortgage companies to advance money at their rate, I think the government will have to lend that money in part directly under Central Mortgage.
It has come to my attention that a considerable amount of United States capital has been available for housing projects in Canada, or would be if those who would provide that capital could be assured that if the projects could be sold they could get the capital and take it back to the United States. At the present time the foreign exchange control regulations permit that, but the foreign exchange control board will give no assurance to United States investors that if they can sell their houses and the money is available they will be able to withdraw that money from Canada. I wonder whether the minister will also speak on that point.

Mr. Chairman, this debate enables one to discuss the housing problem under the minister's estimates. My first words are of congratulation on what the minister has done, particularly for housing in the Toronto area during the period 1949 to 1951 inclusive.
The figures of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation make it clear that for the three-year period, including the years 1949, 1950 and 1951, there will have been erected in the city of Toronto and its immediate surrounding area no fewer than 25,000 new housing units. If one were to take those 25,000 new housing units and place them on lots of standard width, say fifty feet each, he would have 200 miles of new housing units constructed in this three-year period. This means a string of housing units which would go from the outskirts of Toronto easterly to Kingston. I think this illustrates that tremendous things have been done by this government in stimulating housing during the three years in question.
However, although much has been done about the solution of the problem, may I say to the minister that the need is still great
3816	HOUSE OF
Supply-Resources and Development indeed in the metropolitan area of Toronto. We have five emergency housing centres located at Long Branch, Malton, Geco, Stanley Barracks and Lakeside Camp. There are no fewer than 1,010 families located in those emergency housing centres at the present time. These families comprise a group of 5,282 individuals, and only 545 of the 5,282 individuals are relief recipients. And too these individuals are in the centres for the most part through eviction proceedings, and through no choice of their own.
In a recent report of the welfare commissioner for the city of Toronto to the appropriate committee of city council it was said that with reference to those occupants of the emergency housing centres-and I quote the report:
In most instances no other accommodation was available following eviction.
Some had more than one eviction. I think it is also important to place on the record with reference to the Toronto area that at a recent hearing before the new rental board for the province Mr. J. J. Wingfelder, deputy administrator of rentals in Toronto, gave evidence-and indeed it is most cogent. He said:
The housing situation in the Toronto area is terrifying and has not yet reached its peak of seriousness.
With reference to rents Mr. Wingfelder went further. He said that Toronto is an area of highest pressure of rents for all of Canada.
My philosophy teaches me that the home is the backbone of the nation. In my view housing is the natural right of all Canadians. Private enterprise does not always keep pace with the situation, and government aid becomes a necessity.
I commend the minister and the government in that they have placed housing as second only to national defence in Canada. Toronto is an area where we expect to be, and we know that we will be, an arsenal of our preparedness program. It is gratifying today that before the orders of the day were called the minister stated that negotiations were now under way as between this government and the province for perhaps 5,000 housing units to be located in Ontario. We have heard and we believe that these negotiations have to do with 5,000 houses under section 35 of the act. Some will be for rent, and it is important that they should be low-rental houses. Some will be for sale. Others of those units will be apartment units. Let us hope that they can work out an arrangement whereby they will be low-rental apartments.
In the light of my remarks on the seriousness of the situation which exists I hope that the minister will bring to bear


upon the provincial authorities the importance of locating in Toronto our proportionate share of the new housing units rnn the basis of our needs and our population. It will be a sad thing to me if the minister, in his negotiations with the provincial authorities, cannot give us at least 2,000 units in this time of crisis when we have over 1,000 families in these centres, which centres have been called terrifying.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: We are considering item 427, emergency shelter administration, and item 565, dealing with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.

Mr. Chairman, I should like
to ask a question having to do with a project in Vancouver known as the Fraserview project. About two or three years ago the government undertook, through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, to set up this project which was to contain 1,100 homes for veterans.
The whole area which, as the minister knows, is in the city of Vancouver, was expropriated by the government against the wishes of many of the people who had homes in that area. Then the area was resubdivided. Portions of people's orchards and gardens were taken away from them; in some cases their homes had to be moved; and as a result they suffered a great deal of discomfort. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have gone ahead and I believe have finished about 600 of the houses.
Earlier this year it was announced that further development of the plan was to be dropped at least for the time being, with the exception of completing the installation of services such as water, sewers and facilities of that kind. The result is that we have this large area sitting there, all topsyturvy, partially developed, the streets all changed, the parks-which were shown in the lovely plans put out by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation-not put in. Indeed I think the project might properly be described as more or less of a mess. That is the description applied today by some of the people who have written to me asking that something be done to finish off the project.

There have been press reports to the effect that the lots upon which the homes have not been erected might be sold; of course this would mean that in some cases lots taken away from old residents will now be put on the market or turned over to real estate firms, or handed to the city for purposes of sale; the whole project will break down unless the housing corporation completes it.
We are told it has been held up because of the increasing costs, and I have no doubt that costs have gone up. But there seems to be very little prospect of their coming down in the immediate future, and I do suggest to the minister that where a project has been commenced and is well on the way to completion it is very poor business to let it drop when it has reached this stage. Not only is it very poor business, but it is most unfair to the people living in that district, including both the old residents and the veterans who have gone into the new homes which have been completed.
Moreover, it is unfair to the city. The city of Vancouver has co-operated throughout with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I do not believe the minister can have any complaint about the way the city council have acted. But there they are, being criticized by the citizens; yet nothing can be done because the whole scheme is in the hands of the housing corporation. I do not think that is good enough, and I would hope the minister could arrange to have the project completed. In any event I would ask him to let us know what is to be done.

Mr. Chairman, I should
like to say a word, and after I have finished the minister can reply to both the member for Vancouver-Quadra and myself. Before referring to housing in general I should like to refer particularly to the Fraserview project to which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has referred. He gave a broad outline of this project in which some 1,100 homes were to be built. Of these I believe about 600 have been completed and the building of the remaining 500 has been postponed indefinitely. That is the last information I have had in the matter.
As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has pointed out, it is unfortunate that the finishing of this project has been discontinued. It is unfortunate first, because of the great controversy that was created about the project when the land was taken over by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Second, it is unfortunate because of the great need for homes in Vancouver. There was a great deal of vacant tax land in the area, as well as many private homes. The city of Vancouver turned over the tax land 80709-243*
Supply-Resources and Development at a fairly reasonable figure to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, following which proceedings were taken to expropriate the private homes in the area.
There was great protest made when the homes of people who had been established for 25 to 30 years were taken away from them, and their lives upset. I supported the project and tried to make a case-I believe a case could be made-for what Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was doing, in order to provide houses for the people of Vancouver, and of British Columbia generally, where there was such great need. But all the explanations and all the justifications we have made for the-project went by the board when the government, or Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, decided to discontinue building when the project was only half finished. The government has decided to postpone the building of the additional 500 homes, because of increased building costs.
I have a copy of a letter written by the chairman of the Vancouver housing association to the minister. She represented that, even if the cost of each unit should be increased by $1,000 because of increased building costs, at 3J per cent interest and with thirty-five year amortization the increase in rent would only amount to about $5 per month. In view of the terrific need for housing in Vancouver, I suggest that involves a very small amount of money and should not divert the government from its intentions in that particular area.
Let me draw the attention of the minister for a few minutes to the housing situation in Vancouver at the present time. May I first tell him	that there	are still	2,000veterans	families	with four	or	more	smallchildren still waiting after six years for suitable housing accommodation. The building of the 500 houses would provide homes for at least	500, or	a quarter	of	those	2,000veterans	and their families.	At	the end of
1945 the emergency shelter administrator estimated that the shortage of houses in the city of Vancouver amounted to over 23,000 family units. Between 1946 and 1950, both years inclusive, approximately 14,700 housing units were started while the increase in the number of families-and the estimate is a conservative one-was 21,000.
I think the rate of building in Vancouver and British Columbia generally has been higher than in other parts of Canada, but despite the relatively high rate the shortage of houses has increased since the war by a further 6,300 units. Today instead of having a shortage of 23,000 units as we had in 1945 there is the shortage of 30,000, and the population of the city of Vancouver is increasing
3818	HOUSE OF
Supply-Resources and Development every day. In addition the government is making strenuous efforts, and I believe with some success, to bring immigrants to this country many of whom will ultimately reach Vancouver. I think we are seeking trouble if we bring people here without having homes prepared for them and when we have not homes even for the people who are here.
Before I leave the Fraserview project, I suggest to the minister that he give the matter his most earnest consideration before finally deciding not to go ahead with it. I iplead for that because of the controversy that came about as a result of expropriation and the hopes that were raised as to the *development contemplated in that area, one of the finest locations in the Dominion of Canada.
I should like to give the committee the figures as to building progress in Vancouver and greater Vancouver for 1948, 1949 and 1950. Greater Vancouver of course takes in the surrounding municipalities. Dwelling completions in the city of Vancouver in 1948 amounted to 3,391, and in greater Vancouver 6,315. In 1949 completions in the city of Vancouver amounted to 2,748 and in greater Vancouver 5,599. In 1950 completions in the city of Vancouver amounted to 2,271, and in greater Vancouver 4,679. Dwelling starts, buildings started but not necessarily completed, in the city of Vancouver and in greater Vancouver for the same years are as follows: Vancouver in 1948, 3,297, and greater Vancouver, 6,442; in 1949, Vancouver, 2,161, and greater Vancouver, 4,465; in 1950, Vancouver, 2,034 and greater Vancouver, 4,442.
These figures do not include Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation building for which the figures for 1948, 1949 and 1950 are 586, 324 and 294 units respectively, all in the city of Vancouver. I am putting those figures on the record to show that the need for housing both in the city of Vancouver and in the greater area is increasing each year because we are falling further behind each year in the number of homes required. While the need is increasing the number of homes completed and the number of homes started have declined every year from 1948 to 1950. Something must be done. I agree that we must give high priority to our national defence program, but here again I think we are making the greatest mistake we possibly can make if we are going to put everything into the defence program and leave the provision of homes to private enterprise.
It has been demonstrated that for the last twenty-five years private enterprise has not been able to build homes for that section of the community which cannot finance homes for themselves. What is happening today? While low rent homes are what is required,
IMr. Maclnnis.]

it is much easier to get money to build a $15,000 or a $20,000 home than it is to get money to build a $6,000 home. As a matter of fact if we are going to deal with the matter properly I think there should be a maximum limit on the cost of homes, because two homes at $6,000 each are better for the community than one home at $12,000. I suggest that here is a situation that must be dealt with with the greatest possible energy because it is of the greatest possible urgency.
There is one other point I want to bring to the minister's attention. There is another project of 200 homes to be built in the city of Vancouver on the three-way principle under the National Housing Act. The last I heard was that there was a possibility the Little Mountain project would not be proceeded with. I would be very glad if when he speaks the minister would give assurance that this will be gone ahead with at once, and that the Fraserview project will also be completed.

In reply to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, there is very little I can add to the answer I gave to the question he asked in the house on April 9, at which time I told him some 600 odd houses had been completed with another 450 or so to go. We thought the prices for those houses were too high, that there was too big a cushion in them for the contractors, so in fairness to the ultimate tenants who would have to pay the higher costs in terms of rent we let the completion of the project stand in abeyance. We realize that it is very important to complete the project, and we intend to do so. As soon as Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation feels it can get realistic bids for the completion of the remaining houses to round out the project, it will do so.
As for the Little Mountain project, it is out to tender now and it is expected that tenders will be received within the next two or three days. Neither the government of British Columbia nor we have yet seen the tenders, so we are not in a position to say what the costs will be or whether the government of British Columbia will wish to go ahead with it. That is the status of that project.

I wish to take up only two or three minutes of the time of the committee. I listened to the statement of the minister this afternoon, and I was sorry that, like many other hon. members, I was not able to hear all the remarks of the hon. member for Eglinton, owing to the fact that I had to attend a committee.
In dealing with this subject I think we should localize some of our arguments, so for a few minutes I am going to speak of the situation as it exists in the Sarnia district,

one of the fastest growing areas in Canada, which I think every hon. member will agree is making a big contribution to our war effort. There, as we all know, we have the greatest oil refinery in the British empire, which is increasing its capacity by some 25 per cent. There we have the Polymer plant, which is also spending some seven and a half million dollars or so in an expansion program. There we have Canadian Oil coming in, with an eventual program which will cost some $20 million. There we have Dow Chemical, another industry which has contributed much to our war effort, with a $5 million project under way. Sun Oil has a thousand acres or more on which it plans to start a $40 million refinery when steel is available.
I appreciate the difficulties under present conditions, when we have the defence effort competing with the construction industry for available building materials, but I feel that the three levels of government must take steps to bring about a final solution to this problem, which certainly is acute in my area. Let me give one illustration. Just two weeks ago last Saturday night, at eleven o'clock, it became known that a home was available to rent. By twelve thirty some nineteen telephone calls had been received inquiring about that home. That shows how desperate the situation is in Sarnia. I heard what the minister had to say in regard to his chat with representatives of Ontario earlier this week, and I firmly believe there are certain districts in this country to which all levels of government must give special consideration, particularly districts which contribute so much to our defence effort. I believe all hon. members will agree that because of what we produce in Sarnia that is an area which is entitled to special consideration.
I have often thought we are a little slow, not only in this country but in other democratic countries, in carrying on research to find ways of building houses at a lower cost. It seems to me that today Central Mortgage and the loan companies have specifications higher than are necessary. Certainly in some areas they could be moderated, and I believe we will have to moderate those specifications to keep down the cost of building. Perhaps not many people realize what is required to even put up the walls of a house, or the strength of the lumber required to complete a home. I believe these requirements can be modified and costs brought down. It seems to me our research departments could do something, and maybe they are doing more than we think, to bring down these costs.
In our section of the country, and I think this applies elsewhere, we believe that since the new restrictions have been in effect the
1951	3819
Supply-Resources and Development construction of homes has been retarded. In the first place the builder has not been able to obtain a big enough loan to permit him to sell the home with a reasonable down payment. We have not many people in this country today, particularly in my part of it, who can afford to pay $3,000 down on a home they could have obtained a year ago for something like $1,500 down. They are not yet in that bracket, and I do not expect they will be able to afford such down payments. The need for homes is so serious that governments should not delay considering ways-and means of making houses available to-those in the low income brackets. That might be done by increasing the loans, or in someway under section 35 of the act, under which-the three levels of government make-contributions.
Then the higher interest rates, which apparently are inevitable, will be an important factor in the construction and purchase of these homes. There was a day most of us can remember when people built homes to rent, for revenue. That day is gone, I think forever, and today we must make houses available, either for sale or for rent, to those in the low income brackets. I know materials are scarce. As an illustration, my son had intended continuing in the building business after a sojourn elsewhere, but gave up his plan because he could not get rock lath or cement. One dealer had a backlog of fifteen carloads of rock lath, which seems to indicate something wrong with either our production or our distribution. The same thing applies to cement and other materials. I believe the statements made this afternoon as to the increased cost of building were much too conservative. I do not believe we in this country or any other country can depend on those who are engaged in selling building materials in any form to promote research which might lower building costs. That must be done by the government, because today those who have anything to sell can sell it at any price they ask.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am grateful for these few moments, because I have to go to a committee. I am going to make another point which I think will illustrate what I have in mind. Only a few days ago I was talking to one young man who had sold approximately three-quarters of a million dollars' worth of homes in the lower price field, that is between $8,000 and $9,000, during 1950. I was amazed to hear the hon. member who preceded me speak of homes being built for around $6,000. I wish we could build: them for that amount in my area. You might build a three-roomed house for that, but
3820	HOUSE OF
Supply-Resources and Development you would not get much more. This illustration probably is typical of what is happening in many parts of this country. Last Sunday this young man told me that in the two weeks previous he had sold one very poor home, in the newer part of Sarnia which was taken into the city, at a price of $5,200. That was the only sale he had made in two weeks. There are not many people who can pay the higher down payment required to obtain shelter over their heads. In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I believe that the government today must accept a greater responsibility than ever before for housing the people who require shelter.

I am only going to say a few words on this question, Mr. Chairman, as I too have a committee to attend. I listened to the minister's statement this afternoon with a great deal of interest, as I did the statement made by the last speaker. I thought that the minister's statement indicated the great extent to which the government has gone into the field of housing. I believe they have gone a long way since 1946. I might add that I do not have much of a housing problem in my constituency. We solved that problem some considerable time ago through co-operative housing and other methods.
The statement made by the hon. member who just spoke, when compared with what happened in 1946, indicates that the memory of some of the members in this house is rather short. In 1946 the housing field was wide open to the construction industry of this country, known as free enterprise. In that year the government had some control over the distribution of building materials, cement and so forth. A few of us in the house were urging the government to retain that control in the post-war period because we felt more supervision would be required in the sale and distribution of those materials during that period. Many of the hon. members to my right were demanding that the government get back to a normal way of doing things, the law of supply and demand. Slowly but surely the government obeyed that request and unravelled the mechanics of free enterprise. It was very much against our advice.
The statement the minister made this afternoon indicated to me that the government has gone some distance in maintaining the policy they suggested at that time, to the effect that in so far as possible or practicable they would take up the slack where free enterprise failed. The minister's statement definitely shows that they have done that to some extent. It is evident that the hon. 

member who just spoke has changed his opinion completely; he now demands that these materials should be controlled. But that is locking the door after the horse has been stolen. I cannot go along with him. For instance, in the field of housing the construction industry enjoys a rather secure position. They erect a building, and they are guaranteed against loss; money is made available to them. But they want to come in and exact the last pound of flesh.
We are told that an industry is being established in a certain section at a cost of $40 million, but the government is expected to provide housing for the employees. We are going to invent $40 million. We are objecting very strenuously to any excess profits tax. We are not going to contribute anything to the government in the field of taxation, except what we feel is right. But in and around that industry where hundreds of thousands of employees are going to be housed, we expect the taxpayers of Canada to provide the housing. This attitude puts the problem back further than it was fifty or sixty years ago. When the old industries like steel and coal were established in this country, they built houses and rented them to the employees at a nominal figure. After years on that basis, many of these industries passed the houses over to the employees at a very reasonable price. But modern industry is not taking any social responsibility. The social responsibility must be taken by the government, and by the taxpayers of Canada. Unlimited profits they must make, but they object to any suggestion of corporation taxes. Private enterprise must be allowed an open field in so far as profits are concerned, but the building of homes, social responsibility towards the public, that must be accepted by the government. We want government control to the extent of guaranteeing us profits and underwriting our losses, housing our employees, but that is as far as we want government responsibility to go. Do not touch us in the field of taxation. That is the position of the Liberals to some extent, and the Tories to one hundred per cent as indicated by their activities in demanding the removal of controls.
I merely wanted to make these few remarks, Mr. Chairman, because I listened to the minister's statement and I thought it was a very good statement. I believe the government had to go a long way in replacing free enterprise in the field of housing. It is a social responsibility which, in my opinion, develops with industry. I should like to leave this thought with the minister, that housing is one of the first requirements of citizenship.

I do not believe any person can be a good citizen until he drives his roots into the soil and owns a piece of land. I believe the best way to get that type of citizenship is under a co-operative scheme of housing. I do not believe the federal government is doing the right thing when they farm out to insurance companies and large contractors in this country the interest that they have in the building of homes. I believe that money should be made available to the municipalities across the country who plan the housing in the community, who set the taxation rate in that field and who must provide the services.
I think that whole thing should ,be decentralized. Instead of handling the matter through those large financial organizations who have no responsibility socially, who do not want any responsibility to the people as such, except the making of money, I think that process should be reversed and that the municipalities across the country who are with the people, plan for the people, service the people, should be given the money necessary to provide housing in their own communities.
It sounded rather peculiar to me a few minutes ago to hear British Columbia members standing up in this chamber and telling the committee about the terrific shortage of housing there was in the province of British Columbia. British Columbia is the lumber province in Canada. If there is any place in Canada where materials should be available at a reasonable cost, from the hardwood floor to the cement, it is British Columbia. There is something wrong with our planning, Mr. Chairman.
There is no shortage of cement in this country, and there never was. Any time you want to pay an extra 25 cents or 50' cents a bag, and take your cement from the black market, you can get it.
Fifty cents a bag? A dollar a bag.

May I say that you fellows in Ontario are a little bit easier to gyp than we are in the maritimes. It was American cement. There never was any trouble in getting it if you were willing to go on the black market and pay the price. In that field I say that there is a straight monopoly. That is the reason for the situation. There should be some government regulation in the field of supplying the basic materials. There is something wrong in British Columbia when there is a housing shortage. The answer is to provide for the necessary legislation when you are writing amendments to the National Housing Act.
At the present time there is in Nova Scotia a provincial housing act which contains a
7, 1951	3821
Supply-Resources and Development section that enables you to organize co-op. groups and finance the building of co-operative homes at a reasonable cost. I suggest that the National Housing Act should contain a simple provision on a national basis so that where men want to build their own homes it should be done on a national scale through the federal government; there should be a provision similar to the one now contained in the Nova Scotia housing act.
Low-rental housing will never be provided under the present act. The only way to provide it is to do so on a municipal level, through your municipal governments, under a subsidy arrangement with the federal government. If it were done in that way, it would not cost nearly as much money as it does today, with the exorbitant rates that are charged by the people to whom the government is farming out the taxpayers' money.

Mr. Chairman, in the last five years we have heard a tremendous amount of talk about shortages of this and shortages of that, when in reality the true picture is: just let us do a little less work, everybody. That is the true picture. The hon. member who spoke previously talked about British Columbia and why we should never have a shortage of housing. I am sorry that he is not now in the chamber, because I should like to assure him that, even in British Columbia, houses do not grow, irrespective of the amount of timber available there.
Briefly what is wrong in Canada today, in respect of all shortages, is that corporations are making tremendous profits. That' is not the only reason. I am not going to flail the corporations for making tremendous profits. I am only saying that they do so. Evidence of that appears in the papers daily. We read that such-and-such a corporation's profits have doubled, that such-and-such a concern has doubled its capacity. The previous speaker said that the government had gone to a source to distribute money for the building of houses, and he intimated that was not quite the right source, in spite of the fact that the corporation is all set up to loan out money, that that corporation has a tremendous stake in the Dominion of Canada, principally in the life insurance business, in which people have invested millions and millions of dollars, and hope to get them back. Handling money for loan purposes is one source of making legitimate money. There is nothing wrong with that avenue of dispensing money. They probably make a better job of it than the government could, because the government is not set up to lend money by millions for housing. They would have to

Supply-Resources and Development take on more civil servants, something which we are all growling about today. We criticize the government for the tremendous number they are employing. We are all saying they are employing too many, and I believe rightly so.
The truth is that no building materials grow on trees. The truth is that houses will not grow on trees. The truth is that people do not want to work more than eight hours a day, and some are clamouring for shorter hours. That is the truth, and that is why you are short of houses. We are short of cement and we are short of plywood. What is the actual reason for that? Not that the gift of God has not been bestowed on the Dominion of Canada with respect to raw materials. I believe in short hours if there is not enough work to go around. If you can produce what you need for this country in four hours a day, I say: let us work four hours and give everybody an opportunity to work. But I also remember that the Bible says: Six days shalt thou labour and thou shalt rest on the seventh day. I do not think that meant that you shall work four days a week.
As the previous speaker said, what we have got to do is get back to normalcy. Normalcy in the Dominion of Canada is not clamouring for shorter hours. Normalcy is not clamouring for greater pay, or for shorter hours and bigger take-home pay. Let us be men about this matter in the House of Commons and face the facts. You all know in your hearts what the trouble is. It is that we are afraid to work. We are becoming a nation of leaners. Let the people in my constituency-and this applies to every constituency in the Dominion of Canada, particularly in the small municipalities- try to get an American corporation to manufacture something in our town. Try to get an English manufacturing concern to come here, so that Canadians can have the great art of working, and can continue to be carriers of water and tillers of the soil, not participating in the cream of the profits. They will go to the stockholders of the English companies and the American companies, and we will continue to shout about that condition. We are becoming thankful for the fact that we are able to work, let alone make any surplus profit.
That is what is wrong with the Dominion of Canada. The people of Canada are afraid to work; that is, the great majority of them are. There is here in the Dominion of Canada ten hours a day of work cut out for every man who is willing to do it for the same pay he is getting, not overtime.


Let labour buckle down in all walks of life and, where it is necessary, increase then-hours of production.
I have built houses within the last ten years. On one occasion I sold a house. The purchaser was in the furniture business. He had contemplated a trip to British Columbia to see his customers six months previously. He had to move. He was paying $15,000 or $14,500 for this house. He wanted the moving people to move him, his wife and family, on the Saturday afternoon so that they could settle to some extent and order his furniture, and so that he could take the late train on Sunday night for British Columbia in order to carry on his business. Everything was completed except the polishing of the floors by the painters. I asked the painters if they would mind coming back on Saturday morning. Oh, no, they would not come back Saturday morning to help that man, with three children and his wife to get partially settled in their house. They had worked their forty hours a week. The same three gentlemen I have in mind were on relief for five consecutive years; and I am confident that I will live to see the day that the same gentlemen are on relief again, depending on the taxpayers and the good old government. As one woman said to me: I am entitled to a pension; I am entitled to money from the government. I said: "Who do you think the government is? Where do you think they get the money?" She said: "I don't know and I don't care". There is the trouble with the people of Canada. You can spend day in and day out in this House of Commons, one man presenting his views and another one presenting his views, one man saying that labour is not paid enough and another telling them that their hours are too long. Other people are blaming the suppliers of materials necessary for construction. There is not a man, irrespective of what he says in the House of Commons, or the party that he represents, that does not know the truth in his own heart. It is that people will not work long enough hours to produce from the gift of God the necessities of life. That is the trouble; not that you are short of materials, that is, raw materials. You are short of the stomach to work, and it is pretty near time that labour and management got down to the realities of life, put their heads together and said that irrespective of what happens behind the iron curtain or in any other part of the world, we are going to face realities, and if necessary we will work ten or twelve hours a day. When the time comes that we can sleep in bed all hours we shall work

eight hours -a day or four hours a day; but let us get down to it and stop the nonsense.

Mr. Chairman, the subject of national housing has been fairly well discussed this afternoon; therefore I do not think it will be necessary for me to repeat any of the arguments that have already been advanced, consequently my remarks will be very brief at this time. However, I should like to say that I have had some experience in building under the regulations of that National Housing Act. I have been associated with a firm which in the past two or three years has built about 28 houses under the regulations of the National Housing Act, and I can truthfully say that my experience and my association with officials of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have in all ways been very satisfactory.
I should like to take this opportunity to compliment Mr. Douglas, who is in charge of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation office in the city of Edmonton and the surrounding district should like to compliment him on the efficient manner in which he handles the affairs for the corporation in that district. I have always found him very co-operative, always willing to give advice and help with any problem, no matter how large or how small. I think I can also say the same for the insurance companies. The insurance companies with whom I have been mostly associated are the Canada Life Assurance Company and the Manufacturers Life. I have found them very fair to deal with as far as advancing loans under this act is concerned. I have found their inspectors to be very fair, and they always make a thorough inspection, which I would say is to the advantage of everyone concerned, especially to the person who is buying the house after it is completed. Therefore I can truthfully say that my associations under this act have been very satisfactory.
However, I did have some correspondence from some of my constituents, in which they asked a few questions which I should now like to ask the minister. I shall make them very brief, and I hope that he will find time to answer them when he replies to other questions. As I say, these questions arise out of correspondence from my constituents. In the past it has been the practice, I believe, for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to supply contractors with scarce materials such as cement, wiring equipment, plumbing materials and so on, in areas where there is a shortage. Is that still the practice?
My second question is this. What are the regulations in an instance where an insurance company refuses to make a loan under the
Supply-Resources and Development National Housing Act? Suppose a party made application for a loan in an area where an insurance company was already in operation, and for some reason or other the insurance company did not feel that it should grant the loan, not necessarily because the party would not be entitled to the loan but for some other reason, perhaps. What would be the answer in an instance like that?
My third question has to do with the report regarding the curtailment of insurance loans. Is that just a temporary measure on the part of the insurance companies until they have the problem of interest rates adjusted?
These are the three questions which I should like to ask and I hope that the minister will be able to supply me with the information.

The assistance the hon. member referred to was in connection with veterans housing, under which Central Mortgage did provide material on a free issue basis. The corporation also did provide some assistance in supplying nails for a short time under ordinary operations, of the National Housing Act. At the present time there is no such arrangement.
With respect to the operation of insurance companies and their failure to operate in certain instances, the policy of the government and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is that direct loans are not normally made in an area which is usually or normally served by an insurance company.
With respect to the third question, the curtailment of credit on the part of the insurance companies, we hope it will be temporary and that when the amendment to the National Housing Act has been passed by the house to allow for the higher interest rate they will again be in the mortgage field just as they were formerly.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Despite the applause which greeted the remarks that were made by the hon. member for Simcoe North I wish on behalf of the people of Winnipeg North Centre to deny his assertions, and I do so categorically. He made the statement that the real trouble in the country today is that our people are afraid to work, and do not want to work or have not the stomach to work. I have lived all my life either amongst the people of Winnipeg North Centre or amongst people like them. They are the industrial workers to be found in so many of our North American cities. The charge made by the hon. member for Simcoe North does not apply to these people.

It sure does.
3824	HOUSE OF
Supply-Resources and Development

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Not at all, and the hon. member knows it. Not only are they willing to work and work hard, but they have vorked across the years of their lives, except-.ng those days when depressions have robbed them of the chance to work. All they are asking, all we are asking for them when we ask for government responsibility in the field of housing and in other matters of social legislation, is that people who work and produce the wealth of this country, whether it be in the cities or on the farm, have a chance to get back and enjoy some of that wealth.
When we ask for proper housing in cities and in the rural areas of this country we are not asking for something to be picked off trees and given to our people. We are simply asking that the people of this country enjoy what is their right out of the abundance that they produce. It is that philosophy that lies behind the arguments in the field of housing that we have made from this corner of the house across the years, and it is that philosophy which underlies the National Housing Act so far as it goes.
A good deal has been said today, particularly by the hon. member for Spadina, about section 35 of the housing act. The hon. member for Spadina referred to it as one of the most important sections of that act, and in that I agree with him. Section 35 is that section of the National Housing Act which provides for agreements between the federal government and provincial governments on a 75/25 basis for low rental housing projects. As I say, I agree with the hon. member for Spadina as to the importance of that part of our housing legislation, and I share his hope that the minister will be able to persuade the provinces to take greater advantage of it.
I was indeed sorry to note that in the minister's comments today on the workings of section 35 he mentioned a number of provinces, but was unable to make any reference to my own province of Manitoba. There may have been some correspondence, and he may have been in touch with the officials of that province, but it appears that no project under section 35 is under way. I know the city council of Winnipeg has made representations to the provincial government urging that it take advantage of section 35, but as yet nothing has been done.
I would point out that possibly one of the difficulties facing the provinces is that of finding the capital with which to finance their 25 per cent of any of these projects. The hon. member for Spadina this afternoon referred to Alberta as a province which was able to go into this, if it wished to, because it has money; and he indicated that Ontario,


too, has plenty of money. But that does not apply to all the provinces. It is perfectly true that it is no great burden on a province to suffer its 25 per cent share of any loss that may be sustained in the operation of a project under section 35; but, if I understand it correctly, as that section is set up, in order to get going at all the capital has to be put up in the first place. The federal government finds it much easier to obtain its 75 per cent of the capital than many of the provinces find it to obtain their 25 per cent.
I believe discussions have taken place between some of the provinces and the federal government as to the possibility of the federal government's lending that money to the provinces, it still being understood that the provinces would bear their 25 per cent share of any loss sustained. I hope when the minister speaks again he will tell us whether any consideration has been given to that way of making a more effective use of the provisions of section 35.
I was a little disappointed to hear one or two of the minister's comments this afternoon, when he was talking about these dominion-provincial agreements in the field of low-rental housing. If I understood him correctly he said something to this effect, that he was not sure whether low-rental housing projects, which were really low-rental in character, were possible under today's conditions, with particular reference to present high costs.
Well, low and high are relative words; but what struck me about that sentence from the minister was that it seemed to me that he was throwing cold water on these projects which are possible under section 35. I hope he listened carefully when the hon. member for Spadina was speaking, and that he realizes that his job in connection with section 35 is not to say anything that would discourage its use but, rather, to say everything and do everything that he can to encourage its use.
As has been said by other hon. members who have spoken, this is one of the most important parts of the government's housing legislation. It is just about the only part of it in which the element of subsidy enters. The minister will recall that when that section was first proposed the government really took a new forward step in this field, because it indicated its readiness to do something about low-rental housing even though to do so meant providing an element of subsidy.
Our philosophy about housing underlies all of that. We feel that just as it is part of the responsibility of the community as a whole to see that all children have the best

educational opportunities, so in this modern society of ours it is part of the responsibility of the community as a whole, through the governments they elect, to see that all the children, all the workers, all the people enjoy the benefits, not of slums, not of mediocre housing conditions, not of houses which are just roofs to exist under, but of proper housing in the best of communities, that can be planned by modern architects and engineers.
So I strongly urge that the government do everything it can to push the use of section 35 of the National Housing Act. I urge that consideration be given to the proposal that ways and means be found of lending money to the provinces to find that 25 per cent of the capital they must put up. I urge that consideration be given to changing that figure, if that is necessary. Perhaps 75/25 is not the proper relationship; maybe it should be 80/20, 85/15, or even 90/10. The government is into this business of being concerned about housing. It is a social responsibility and a national responsibility, and a good step has been taken. Let it not be nullified by apathy on the part of the government.
Another phase of the matter which was discussed today-and I shall take only a moment or two to speak about it-has to do with the question of the withdrawal of the provision for the additional one-sixth that was announced earlier this session. That has prevented many people from getting a sufficient loan to get started, and I do hope steps will be taken soon to restore to its maximum the amount of the mortgage that can be obtained under the National Housing Act. I know the idea was to restrict housing, because of certain shortages of building materials. Surely if housing is to be restricted it should be on some basis other than that of the size of the pocketbooks of those needing houses.
Then, with respect to another matter, namely the increase in the interest rate from 4J to 5 per cent, I am afraid I cannot agree with the hon. member for Spadina, with the minister and with others who have expressed a similar view, that this might help the situation. It seems to me that what is needed in this field of building new homes is something of the same philosophy that the government has accepted with regard to homes for rent.
Here, too, the element of subsidy must enter, and I am satisfied that the day will come, because of our sense of social responsibility in respect of housing, that we will introduce an element of subsidy into the assistance we provide by way of help in building new homes. One of the ways that can be done is by making money available,
Supply-Resources and Development not at the rate of interest which can be obtained by investors of private funds who invest their funds for making profit, but at rates of interest which approximate the actual cost of lending money.
I must not get into a speech on financial or monetary policy, but it does seem to me that what we should be doing is not raising interest rates that the National Housing Act permits to insurance and loan companies, but rather we should be lowering that interest rate, even if it means that the government itself, directly or through the Bank of Canada, must actually lend money directly for the building of houses. If the government lends money for that purpose at a rate less than the market rate for invested money it is true that will be to a certain extent subsidizing the building of new homes, but I submit that is every bit as good as subsidizing the production of gold and a lot of other things we subsidize in this country. In fact the providing of homes is one of our greatest national social responsibilities, and I urge consideration of that phase of the matter.
Several members who have risen to their feet tonight have indicated that they had to leave to go to committees, and there are indeed quite a few committees meeting. One who had to go to a committee before he could get a chance to speak was my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West. Just before he went he said there was one point that he would like to see given expression to in the course of the debate tonight. As a matter of fact it is a view I would be very happy to express myself, and I do so not only on my own behalf but on his behalf. He pointed out, as other members in the house have pointed out from time to time, the difficulty that people in small unincorporated communities, villages, and so on, have in getting the benefit of our federal legislation. This legislation is not only for the cities. It is not only for larger centres. It should be for all Canadians. If the insurance and loan companies do not feel that way about it, if they do not want to make their money available to help people to have decent homes in the rural areas and in small unincorporated communities, I submit there again the argument is strong that the government should step in directly. I make that plea on behalf of the hon. member for Kootenay West because he had to go to a committee, and I support it most strongly myself.
There is just one other comment I wish to make, and it relates again to something that the minister talked about in his remarks this afternoon. He referred to the fact that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at one time had some 53,000 rental units. He

Supply-Resources and Development indicated that some 30,000 of those had been offered for sale and that 27,000 had been purchased. I believe he gave some other figures, but that is enough for now. I take it that the reference in that statement is in the main to wartime houses that have been sold to veterans. I would have to admit from the large number who have purchased these homes that there must be many who feel satisfied with that program of the government.
I must tell the minister, however, that I am still receiving complaints about this program from various parts of the country. Earlier this session I drew to his attention complaints from the Winnipeg branch No. 1 of the Canadian Legion. I have since had occasion by correspondence to draw to his attention complaints from places like Brantford and Paris in Ontario, again from veterans organizations. Only two or three days ago I wrote him on behalf of another branch of the Canadian Legion in northern Ontario. I could mention other places, such as Regina, Fort William and other cities.
In all these cases the complaint is the same. Veterans who have been renting these houses for a period of time and have enjoyed the benefit of lower rent than they might have had elsewhere are being pressed by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to purchase these homes. In some cases when they are not able to purchase the homes they are occupying they find that other veterans come along and purchase them, and the veterans who are in them have to move elsewhere. It makes one wonder just how many of those who have purchased these homes did so under pressure. The veterans in these organizations in the centres I have named, and in other centres, feel that they are being treated unfairly in this respect. They hear a great deal being said about the desirability of low rental housing projects, about projects of this kind that enable people to live in quarters that they can pay for within their means. But here you have a program like that being upset by the policy of the government at the present time.
I agree with the hon. member for Spadina that these matters with respect to wartime housing and with relation to emergency housing only touch the fringe of the problem, and that our real effort should be concentrated not on them but on ways and means designed to build permanent housing for the people of this country, and let it be housing of a kind that our people really deserve.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure from the remarks I have made previously


on this subject it is well known how concerned I am about the housing situation in the city of Hamilton. In a local newspaper the other evening there was a dispatch from Ottawa claiming that the Minister of Defence Production has authority under recent legislation to assist companies to build houses in communities where defence contracts have produced an acute housing shortage. I have noticed at various times that in articles appearing in the press with reference to the housing situation in Canada, and in particular with reference to the communities where defence activities are producing a bad housing situation, the name of the city of Hamilton rarely appears. Two or three of the larger cities appear but in the city of Hamilton we have a situation that has developed over many years and, while I dare say it is similar to that which obtains in other centres, it is nevertheless aggravated by many factors.
I should like to quote from a very interesting report on housing presented at the annual meeting of the Canadian welfare council by a member of the Hamilton body. She says in part:
. . . poor housing has been a chronic state in many parts of Canada for many years. With the first world war families began to crowd into the city areas and the need to house this influx was not adequately met before the onrush of the depression meant the doubling up of families who could not afford to keep up separate establishments. Besides, there was no money available for building, either for rent or sale. Then came the next war with its shortages of building materials on one hand and the rapidly growing number of new families on the other. Post-war has brought steadily rising costs and now again we are being faced with an increasing shortage of materials with a result that the gap between needs and available supply is widening rather than decreasing.
After some general comments she goes on to speak about Hamilton in particular and gives some very pertinent figures. She says:
In Hamilton we have about 1,600 wartime houses with on an average of one coming free every month. On the waiting list they accept only veterans with children and on the list at the present time there are 603 families wanting to rent and over 1,000 wanting to buy. Here are a minimum of 1,600 families (for it does not include nonveterans) seeking what they consider adequate accommodation at a reasonable rent. Some are separated with all the loss of daily living together that means an impoverishment to both the parents and children, not to mention the possibility of the weakening of the tie between them and the beginning of a loss of responsibility. Some are living with relatives which can usually only provide a satisfactory solution for a short period of time. Such a situation is full of potential danger to the development of healthy families.
In reference to this lady's statement that a thousand people want to buy houses at the present time, I should like to go back to the day in this house earlier in this session

when the minister announced the curtailment of the loans of one-sixth. I recall that I was amazed and greatly concerned over what I was sure would happen; and today in our city an investigation is going on which has broken into the headlines of our newspapers, with rather pitiful photographs. The one I now hold in my hand is of two small children, I would judge about three years of age, tied to a telegraph pole. They live in a highly congested area where the street, and a very busy street at that, is the only playground. So they will not be run over by the traffic, their mother ties them to the telegraph pole every day when they go out to play.
A few moments ago the minister spoke about the action to be taken shortly in connection with raising the interest rates. This article also mentions that, and says that in the meantime advances on mortgages have been frozen, with the result that builders are starved for ready cash and will be starved until the move is approved, which the writer guesses will come up in the house about July 1. I should hope that whatever is holding up the cash advances on these mortgages might be dealt with expeditiously so the work can proceed. It is estimated by the builders in Hamilton that only about 300 units will be built there in 1951, with over 1,600 families needing homes immediately. Only 51 dwellings were started in January of this year. I do not have the figures for the subsequent months, but with the mortgage money being frozen for the time being I do not suppose they are very cheerful.
I have more articles and more pictures which I would be glad to send to the minister, though I dare say he gets them from every city in Canada. In his statement this afternoon the minister said:
We will pay particular attention to the communities where housing is most needed. Because defence production is the main effort of the country today the government is anxious to do everything it can to meet the housing needs in defence production areas.
Whatever consideration is being given to making it easier for builders to build and for workmen to own their own homes, I do hope special attention will be paid to Hamilton. There we have this situation, that not only are all these people seeking homes but in some districts existing homes are actually being removed to make way for expanding industry. In one section 250 people are being put out of their homes for this reason. We have the loss of this housing accommodation, and we have all these people coming to Hamilton now to work in our defence plants.
Supply-Resources and Development These industries are by no means at their peak; this is only the beginning. We have this backlog of housing, as I quoted from the report, which goes back even to the first war days, and the situation is being further aggravated by the destruction of existing homes. I cannot too strongly urge the minister to give special attention to this city, because I know that from Hamilton must come a large part of the defence production which may ultimately save this nation.

Perhaps I should say a word in reply to the hon. member for Hamilton West and tell her that though the situation is very difficult, and no one overlooks the seriousness of the housing situation in her city, I hardly think she was justified in remarking that she doubted whether 300 houses would be built in Hamilton this year. The statistics show that 433 houses were started in the first five months of this year as against 307 last year, and that in the metropolitan Hamilton area there have been 800 completions so far this year as against 485 last year. Houses under construction at the present time number 881 as against 806 at the same period last year.

I did not know how
many had been started this year. I am pleased to hear that the number is over 400, but even that is merely scratching the surface. We do have in Hamilton, or will have as soon as this trunk sewer on the mountain is finished, a large area which can be serviced very quickly. That is a situation which has not obtained for some time.
I did not mean to imply that the problem had been solved; I just wanted to say it was considerably better than the 300 the hon. member mentioned.

I want to bring to the attention of the minister a problem which is causing a great deal of dismay in many municipalities. I refer to the rapid increase in municipal taxation. There is no question but that we need every house we can possibly build. There is no question but that we should have a greater house-building program. But there is another problem which is ancillary to the general problem of the construction of houses, particularly low rental houses and more particularly houses assisted under any government scheme; that is the servicing of those houses after they are constructed, through municipal taxation.
This is a terribly serious matter. Municipal taxation is different from any other type of taxation because it destroys the asset you have. If in one year the tax on your house is X units and it goes up to X plus 20, X plus

Supply-Resources and Development 50 and so on until it gets to 2X units, the value of your house is considerably less than half its value before the increase in taxation. Under our federal and provincial system of government municipal taxation is caused by the essential services which must be provided by the municipality, such as schools, streets, lighting, sidewalks, sewers and all the other things that must go to service a house. They are as essential as the bricks and mortar, the floors and the roof that go to make up the house, and in my contention they should be considered part of the cost of building that house. Many communities have been ruined because a housing scheme has increased taxes through the necessity of building more schools, roads and the hundred and one other things that must be provided. The old residents in that community will then have had their investment impaired, and the value of their houses considerably lessened by the new housing project.
A year or so ago, Mr. Chairman, I suggested that in order to relieve the burden of municipal taxation, municipal taxes might be considered as a deduction of income for income tax purposes. I still think that was a good suggestion, and would have helped considerably. However, the problem we face today is that municipalities, both large and small, particularly in the province of Ontario, are confronted with a serious physical problem owing to the number of new dwelling houses that have been built. I wonder if the minister has considered any of the following things? First of all, when a new housing project is being built with federal assistance, is the community in which it is going stabilized, that is, is the ratio of industry to domestic houses such that tax increases will be equitably borne by both industry and domestic dwellings; does the community in which these houses are being placed have any type of town planning to ensure that the location of the new housing units will be maintained as a proper housing area and not become blighted through industrial development?
These things are very important, Mr. Chairman, not only to the individuals who live in these communities, but to the government to safeguard its investment. I should like to see some provisions in the housing act to the effect that only in properly planned communities would assistance be given. I am sure that in the long run this would be of benefit to all, because if you have an unplanned municipality and you have an addition of hundreds of houses, you are going to upset the equilibrium of that municipality. Then, instead of producing an asset, you may produce a great liability, a liability not only
tMr. Adamson.]

to the people already living in the municipality but to the very people you want to help. If a house is built in an unplanned district, the district might deteriorate and the investment of the home owner would deteriorate along with the district.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that the minister will be able to do something in this regard, because I sincerely believe that a properly planned community is the best safeguard, not only for the government but for the home owner whom we wish to help.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that everyone was impressed by the minister's statement this afternoon. It sounded to me as though the minister had been responsible for many improvements, and for increasing the number of houses through the facilities provided by the act. It came to me somewhat as a shock to hear the hon. member for Spadina state that the housing shortage is greater now than it was in 1944. There is now a shortage of about 700,000 houses. If that is so, then there is some truth in the statement of the hon. member for Eglinton that housing is the No. 2 problem of the nation. It ranks next to the question of defence.
If that is so, Mr Chairman, then I feel that perhaps this committee has not been giving the attention to this subject which it deserves. I cannot speak for any other community than the one I represent. I know the minister is familiar with that community. He has been there, and he has seen the problem for himself. I believe he will recognize that there is a problem in St. John's which is only being scratched at the present time. He spoke of 140 units, but I did not hear him say that they had been completed. I heard the member for Spadina say they had been completed. They were in the process of erection when I saw them in January, and I am glad to hear they have now been finished.
I do not know what arrangement was made for putting people into them. I understand that instead of being a low-cost rental proposition the houses will be rented for $40 per month. I do not believe that many of the poor people in the slum areas would be able to occupy those houses and pay that amount of money. I do not want to prolong this debate unnecessarily, but I would point out that one section of St. John's was destroyed by fire in 1892.
