The part west of the line where the fire took place is very old and has to be renewed. I believe the municipality is now tearing down some of those houses. We have three main problems down three, and one is slum clearance. The province has adopted something of that nature, but we have to have new houses in which people can live.
382S

It seems to me that once before, Mr. Chairman, you prevented me from speaking about the terrible conditions in the slum area of St. John's. I must repeat that those are serious, and no honest man can feel happy about those conditions under which the people are living. I suppose there are places in this capital city of Ottawa where people are living in such conditions that we would be ashamed to let outside people know about them.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member to remind me of the circumstances in which I prevented him from discussing this matter?

We were discussing this subject before, Mr. Chairman, and I was speaking about the hardships of the people who live under poor housing conditions in St. John's. I believe the chairman thought I was harrowing the feelings of the members of the house, and perhaps might harrow the feelings of the people who live in those houses. 1 believe you should recall the incident, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: If you will pardon me, I do not. I should like to inform the hon. member that at the time I interrupted him when he was speaking about slum conditions in St. John's I did so because I considered he was not in order. In any event, I shall look up the matter. I do not believe the hon. member should say that at one time or another I prevented him from discussing a certain subject if he was in order.

The main point is that we have these conditions from one reason or another, and they ought to be removed. The question arises, whose responsibility is it? Is it the responsibility of the municipality, the province or the federal government? It seems to me it is a joint responsibility of the three forms of government. The minister has authority under the act to conduct research and investigation, I am wondering if he has been carrying on any investigations in the city of St. John's? It seems to me that city is so situate that we could have an ideal city there. An enormous amount of work has to be done before the city can be called an ideal city. I am wondering if the minister has been giving sufficient attention to the conditions as they exist there. The city is greatly congested. As he knows, the houses are mostly of wooden construction, built side by side, largely in long rows of ten, fifteen, twenty and perhaps even more than that, with narrow streets. A beginning is now being made to eliminate the worst places. I trust that some kind of plan will be devised so that, when houses
7. 1951
Supply-Resources and Development are being constructed in the area which is being cleared, they will be of a different type and provision will be made for playgrounds and parks. That is one of the problems that I think should be a matter of study by the officials of the minister's department.
There is another problem that exists in Newfoundland about which I think the minister may perhaps not be aware. I do not believe there are many places outside of the cities or large towns, where a loan is being granted by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. On behalf of one fisherman living in my constituency I made application for a loan to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation agent down there, and it was turned down. It might have been turned down for some other reason than that it was in a rural area. But I do not believe that any effort is being made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to make these loans available to that class of person where he wants to build a house or where he wants to improve it or enlarge it. Only the other day a lady wrote to me to see if she could obtain a loan for the completion of the house which the husband had built. I consulted with the officials of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and I was told that no loan was available for that type of thing. Yet I find in the act, under the section dealing with home improvement loans or home extension loans, that such a loan can be made. I do not know whether any regulation has been made to prevent it. But that is the information I obtained from the agent in St. John's and from the office here in Ottawa. It seems to me that more consideration should be given to the people who live outside the cities. The trust companies will not lend them any money; and if the federal government will not lend them any money, they are under a great handicap, and what they are really doing is contributing for the benefit of other people, because in paying taxes they are helping to make loans to people who live in cities. Surely the minister will 'give that matter consideration. But it seems to me that overriding all that-and it is the principal thing I have to say-if the problem is so serious and we are slipping behind, and have slipped behind another 50,000 homes in the past five or six years, the minister would be justified in setting up a commission to deal with this problem for some years ahead. We have had a royal commission on the arts and sciences. We have had a committee of this house doing wonderful work in connection with old age pensions -which are going to cost the government hundreds of millions of dollars a year. We have had a royal commission on transportation. But was any one of those



Supply-Resources and Development commissions or committees concerned with anything more important than the housing problem in this country? I am sure the minister will agree with me that the housing problem should be tackled now. It should not be allowed to slip back, because it will slip back faster during these war years, or these years of tension, if we neglect it. I urge upon the minister that he not allow his colleagues in the government to give the matter of housing a place too far back when considering matters of policy.

In his initial statement this afternoon the minister spoke with a considerable amount of satisfaction about the sales which had been made of wartime housing units. I can assure him that that is not a satisfaction which is shared by a considerable number of the veterans in Calgary at least, or by some, I think, in other places. Earlier this evening some reference was made to this matter, but I should like to deal with it from a slightly different point of view.
What is actually happening or what has happened in several cases in Calgary is that people who bought these wartime houses have now moved out of them and are renting them to other people at $70 and $80 and $90 a month. In the meantime, they have moved into other houses themselves which they have bought in some cases. That is the situation in at least two cases that I know of. Naturally that procedure makes for bad feeling amongst the many hundreds of veterans who are without houses, who were on the waiting list for some years, in some cases, waiting to get into one of these wartime houses.
The first question I should like to ask the minister is whether there is any means whatever that his department can put into effect to prevent this sort of thing from going on; I refer to the situation of a person getting into one of these houses, buying it and turning around and renting it to somebody else at a high rent; because in Calgary housing is extremely short, the people are desperate, and these high and excessive rents can be secured. It may be a thing which would be rather difficult to stop, but I would think that when one of these wartime houses is sold to the tenant who is in it, a provision could easily be put in the contract to the effect that there would be no what you might call renting it out at a high level. Surely it would be possible to put into effect some safeguard to prevent this abuse from going on. It is an abuse which I think causes an unnecessary amount of bad feeling.
In addition to that, I should like to ask the minister whether the tenants in these houses are being put out or whether there is any intention of putting them out if they have

no other place to go. In his statement this afternoon the minister said that, as to tenants who did not wish to buy-and the ones who do not wish to buy are mostly those who just cannot raise the down payment with which to buy, they are in such bad circumstances- when the house they are in is sold they are put into another house owned by Wartime Housing. I should like to find out if that is always the situation. Amongst these people in Calgary who are in the position of not being able to buy their houses, there is certainly quite a strong rumour going around to the effect that if they do not buy them by October they are likely to be out of luck. The word that goes around there is: Make sure that you get your house bought before October or you are likely to find yourself out on the street, come next spring in any event. I should therefore be obliged to the minister if he will make a statement with regard to those three questions that I have asked. I should also like to say at this time that I think that this policy being followed by the government of getting rid of these wartime houses as rapidly as possible was probably a mistake, in view of the present housing situation. I should like to ask whether they intend to sell all those houses or whether there is any intention of holding a certain number of them to look after what we might perhaps call some of our neediest cases among the veterans.

I have three questions I should like to ask, and the minister can answer them briefly. He told us he had built 140 new houses in Newfoundland this year, I believe. I wonder where they were built, or where the building sites were. Can he tell me anything about the demand, how great the demand is? Has the cost of building changed any? I refer to the actual cost.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Before the minister replies, may I be permitted to deal with the remark that was made a moment ago by the hon. member for St. John's West when he spoke of slum clearance and when he said that I as chairman prevented him from discussing that subject, on a previous occasion. The committee will recall that I rose at that time and said that if I had stopped him it was probably because I considered that while he was discussing slum clearance, he was out of order. I now have Hansard showing what happened at that time. It is found at page 2444 of volume III of the second session of 1949. The committee will bear with me. It is very important that this point should be cleared up. It reads as follows:

I should like to
clear up a few points with regard to what my colleague has said about this section. It is rather

difficult to approach the matter in view of the answer just given by the minister. I would certainly ask his sympathetic consideration if the subject ever comes to his attention. I understand the minister has been in St. John's, and has seen the conditions prevailing in certain sections of the city. There is a historical explanation of those conditions.
St. John's was destroyed by fire in 1846, and wooden houses were built. In 1892 half the city was destroyed by fire, and the half that remained'-which covers about 50 acres-is in a bad condition owing to overcrowding. During the first and second world wars, people went to live in areas known as Southside hill and Blackhead road. The area is really in a scandalous condition. No interest is being taken in these people. In two sections of the city at least there is certainly a need for a housing project. If I could describe truthfully the condition-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I must ask the hon.
member to confine his remarks to the clause under discussion. His remarks must be strictly relevant to the clause.

Surely, Mr. Chairman, when we are speaking on a housing project we must say why it is that we need one. I hope the minister is not objecting to my drawing these things to his attention. He may have forgotten them in his hurried1 visit, but I am closely associated with them. I have been closely associated with these conditions for a great many years.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
That cannot be done
under this section. We are now discussing section 9.

The minister
said it could. He told us that a slum clearance project could be considered under this section because it is a project arranged between-

No, Mr. Chairman. I think I should clarify that point. I said that slum clearance and this section could be regarded as complementary projects. But this section has nothing whatsoever to do with slum clearance as such. Slum clearance is covered under an entirely separate section of the National Housing Act.

Since the minister gave me that answer some time ago, I have read the section and I think the position is this.
Then he carried on, but he did discuss the matter of slum clearance again, and there was a point of order raised by the minister. Therefore, I say it is clear from the record that when I asked the hon. member for St. John's West not to discuss slum clearance it was because I considered that in doing that he was out of order.
When the hon. member for St. John's West reads the remarks that I have made following his this evening I hope that he will follow the only course which is proper in the circumstances.

The hon. member for York West raised one or two questions, and perhaps I should deal with them. His great concern was about town planning. I might say that is a great concern of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation as well. There is a town planning section in the act, and they have a town planning division in the corporation. Where projects are concerned, which I imagine is what the hon. member had primarily in mind, it can be
Supply-Resources and Development taken for granted that unless there is adequate planning the project does not proceed. However, I should say that the main approach to the problem now is under section 35 of the housing act where the proposals and the planning come from the province, and it goes forward only on a joint agreement basis. However, we are very strong supporters of town planning, and we think that where possible it should be adhered to.
On the point raised by the hon. member for Calgary East, there are circumstances in which houses sold to veterans are in turn resold, and I would imagine that the rents charged are perhaps higher than would have been charged had the house remained in the hands of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
For war workers' houses where they are sold to a civilian there is an arrangement under the agreement whereby if the purchaser retains occupancy for a period of five years he gets a preferred purchase right, which is an inducement and prevents that sort of traffic, you might say, that the hon. member had in mind.
That does not prevent renting the house.

The fact of the matter is that he must have occupancy himself for a period to earn the preferred purchase price. There is no such arrangement, however, for veterans houses, and they can indulge in rerenting, as the hon. member has pointed out.
The sales program to which he referred has been going well. I think the hon. member asked whether or not there were cases where veterans were put out of a house and no suitable replacement provided for them. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation knows of no single instance, and I know of no single instance, where a veteran was not re-accommodated within the project area, and there have been no major difficulties in that regard.
The houses made available for sale are those up to and including the 1947 program where the arrangements with the municipalities have permitted it, and where suitable arrangements have been made with municipalities.
The hon. member for St. John's East referred to housing conditions in St. John's and, as I understood him-and I did not understand him too clearly-asked whether the demand for houses in St. John's is still strong and what is the relationship between costs now and costs a year ago.

Not only in St. John's, but throughout the province generally.

Supply-Resources and Development
The demand for housing is of course still strong, and roughly speaking the costs now are about 15 per cent higher than they were a year-ago.

I should like to thank the minister for the answer he gave me to my questions, and to ask him also if there is any truth whatever in the story which is circulating very strongly that October is the deadline for people in those houses to buy them.
There is no truth in that statement.

There is one other question the minister did not answer. I asked where these houses were built and where the building lots were said to be. Are they all in St. John's or in other parts of the province?
The project which the hon. member referred to is the Ebsary estate in St. John's.

There is one other question I asked which the minister did not answer. Is Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation proceeding to sell all of these rental houses, or are they going to retain a certain number to look after what you might call the most needy cases of veterans needing rental houses?

I answered that, I think, only indirectly. I did say that up to and including the 1947 building program all the houses are being made available for sale, where that is permitted under the agreement with municipalities, and where suitable arrangements have been worked out with municipalities. Houses built for veterans since that time have not yet been made available for sale.
How many houses would that leave since 1947 in Calgary which would still be available for rental purposes?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Give it for Regina and Winnipeg as well.
Perhaps we can look that up and give it to the hon. members before we pass from housing altogether.

Can the minister tell us
whether there has been any change in the attitude of lending companies since the announcement of the increased rate in interest? Are they still reluctant to lend?

They of course are not in a position to lend now. The amendment has not been dealt with by parliament. We understand, however, from talks with them that, once the legislation is enacted, they will be in the mortgage field and will carry out their lending program.

Could they not do it under
the old plan? There is nothing to stop them from lending under the old plan?

The reason we had to seek
an amendment to the act was that they were no longer lending under the old rate of interest of 4J- per cent. But we believe and we hope that they will return to a lending program at the new rate of interest, once this amendment has been passed.

Can the minister say
why lending companies with offices in Ottawa refuse to lend money to builders across the river?
I do not know the particular circumstances, but I would imagine the lending institutions are exercising their privilege of making loans to the best advantage, where they can.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Are there any agreements
pending between the government of Manitoba and the federal government under section 35 of the housing act?
No, there are not.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Have there been any discussions as to possible agreements?
To my knowledge, sir, there have been no discussions since the discussions we had with them at the time we were considering changes to the act, which ultimately resulted in the passing of section 35.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I take it from those answers that the government of Manitoba has not made an approach to the federal government. Is the federal government doing anything further to try to sell this idea to the provinces, such as Manitoba?

Well, in view of the responsibilities various levels of government have for this problem of housing, we do not feel it would be appropriate for the federal government to put on a strenuous sales campaign to induce a province to enter into any program that is primarily its responsibility. But we have, in various public statements, on very many occasions, said that section 35 was available to anyone who wished to submit proposals that would meet with the mutual satisfaction of all levels of government concerned.

While the Minister of
Finance is in his seat, perhaps he could assist the Minister of Resources and Development in answering a question I raised this afternoon. I pointed out that, to my knowledge, there is American capital available for building in Canada, provided some assurance could be given that if investments

could be liquidated within a given period of two or three years the original capital could be taken back to the United States.
I have before me the regulation of the foreign exchange control board which states:
A non-resident who makes a new capital investment in Canada (other than in marketable securities) and records the investment with the board when it is made, is permitted under the policy followed by the board at present, subsequently to liquidate the investment in Canada and withdraw the proceeds from Canada.
But the foreign exchange control board can give no assurance that that policy may not be changed without notice at any time. Can either of the ministers tell us why that could not be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I should answer the question. It has been the policy of the board for a good many years. On important matters of this kind one can never and probably one should not ever give a positive assurance as to what might have to be done under other circumstances. My recollection is that even in the latter days of the war we allowed new investments of that kind-that is, post-September 1949 investments-to be taken out by the investors. But circumstances might be such that it would be necessary to impose very much more drastic exchange regulations. I do not contemplate for a moment that it would be, because the whole trend in recent years has been to relax. But the outside investor, of course, has to take his chances on it.

I should like to ask the minister, following his reply concerning this business of people buying these wartime houses and then renting them at high prices and using the proceeds to build other houses for themselves, if any consideration has been given by his department to safeguards which would prevent that very abuse from taking place.

I have the figures for the houses that will remain in Calgary, and also in Regina and greater Winnipeg, if all the houses up to and including the 1947 program are sold. In other words these houses on the 1948-49 programs number:	Calgary, 300;
Regina, 147; and greater Winnipeg, 1,415.
Then, on the other point to which the hon. member for Calgary East referred, I would say that this is a matter that has been receiving consideration. It is known that what the hon. member has described as an abuse does take place. It is difficult to cope with when Central Mortgage and Housing sells a house to a veteran and gives him title. Normally one would consider the veteran is free to do with his property what anyone else would
7, 1951	3833
Supply-Resources and Development do with property acquired under a similar transaction. However, I can say that the matter is one of concern and consideration; but beyond that I have nothing to say.
You have no answer to it yet, do you mean?

Has the minister any information regarding the number of times that veterans who cannot buy their houses are asked to move, in this process of selling veterans' houses? My attention has been called to one or two cases where not only the first but the second house was sold, and the veteran had the idea that he had to keep on moving so long as the house he occupied was saleable. Is there any information on that point?

The instances concerning
which we have immediate knowledge are very few. There are not more than two or three such instances. We would have to search the records for an accurate number. Anyway it is a very small number, indeed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Only two or three instances where the same veteran has had to move twice? Is that what the minister means? Surely there are more cases than that where the veteran has had to move because the house has been sold.
Two or three instances where he has been obliged to move once, and then the house to which he moved has been sold. I understood that was the nature of the hon. member's question.

One case in particular in connection with the sale of veterans wartime housing in Calgary has come to my attention. I took this up with the government and I must say a very satisfactory settlement was made.
In general the complaint was that some of these veterans have been living in wartime housing the government decided should be sold. It now appears that some agents are coming to veterans who moved into these houses and are telling them that unless they are prepared to buy them right away they will be kicked out on the street. Those are the words that were used.
I understand that is not the policy of the department. It is my understanding that if these people cannot buy the houses in which they are living, they are not to be kicked out. In the case I brought to the minister's attention it worked out so that these people, after having been informed they were going to be kicked out if they did not buy the place, are now assured that they are going to be able to live in that house. I think there should be some regulation governing the

Supply-Resources and Development attitude of the inspectors who go around to the veterans giving them such information. It not only instils a great deal of fear in the people who are living in these houses hut it gives the department a bad name because in these cases the department itself must take that responsibility. Is there anything being done by the department to notify these people now living in wartime houses, and who cannot possibly raise the down payment-I think it is 10 per cent-that they are not going to be kicked out, that they do not need to worry, and that as time goes on they will be given every opportunity to purchase the house if they can raise the down payment? It would certainly do a lot to relieve the anxiety of some of these people living in these houses.

I think that question was
dealt with in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Calgary East. I know of no instance in which a veteran was told that if he did not buy the house he would be kicked out.
I drew a case to the attention of the department.

We have been informed at
various times that people dealing with the sales program have been harsh in their language, and on investigation we have always found that they have never been quite as harsh as had been represented to us. Nevertheless in all instances Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been very anxious that there shall be none of that aggressive approach to the problem. They have cautioned their people. They have emphasized the element of good will, and I believe in the over-all picture they have been successful in achieving pretty good public relations.
I want to assure the minister that I was not misrepresenting the case. I took it up with his parliamentary assistant and it was very satisfactorily settled.

Can the
minister tell me whether they have made any study in the city of St. John's with regard to housing needs?

The problem in St. John's
is well known to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. They have been over it a great many times with the Hon. Mr. Vardy, minister without portfolio in the Newfoundland government, who is responsible for housing. The local Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation officials are fully familiar with it, and I think that in brief the question can be answered in the affirmative.

I did not get the minister's answer to my question. How many veterans have had to move once because the houses they occupied were being sold, and how many veterans have had to move more than once because the second houses were sold?

The answer is something
that I can get only after having the records searched. We would not have the information available at the present moment. Would the hon. member be satisfied if I give him that information on a subsequent occasion?
Thank you.

I have not been able to
be present during the discussion, and I trust I shall not be repeating. However, so far as I can see, we seem to have got ourselves into a dead end street here and there in discussing the matter of housing and finding a solution. One of the difficulties appears to be that some provinces are hesitant about entering into agreements. Could the minister give the committee some sort of idea as to what seems to be the main reason or reasons why the provinces hesitate to enter into these agreements? It is granted that they realize that housing is their responsibility and that they are anxious to improve housing. The provinces must be just as anxious to improve housing conditions as anybody could be, and the same must be true of the municipal authorities. What seems to be the difficulty in the way?

I think perhaps the various provinces approach the problem in various ways. I of course would not presume to speak for them or to represent to this house what they regard their difficulties to be. I would imagine the hon. member has in mind particularly the province of Alberta. They are one of the provinces that did not pass complementary legislation to enable them to enter into arrangements under section 35 of the National Housing Act. We have had some discussions with them about participation under the act. They have their own views on how housing should be developed and what steps should be taken with respect to it. I certainly believe they have honest views. There is no question on that point, but the fact of the matter is that until recently they have not taken steps to qualify themselves for participation under section 35. Recently they did indicate an interest, and we told them that we would be very happy to receive specific proposals from them. However, I would imagine that before they can participate they would have to do something about their legislation.
tMr. Johnston.]
There is no general statement that could apply to the majority of the provinces?
No.

They do not tell the
minister they are afraid to take hold of the thing for fear they will be unable to finance it?
No, there has been no such general statement.

It seems to me in listening to the discussion and attending to it as far as I have' been able to be in attendance-and I should like to congratulate the minister on the hopeful attitude he manifested in his original statement-that we are confronted with certain frustrations in our efforts to provide the housing that everybody desires to provide in this country. The first one is the indisposition of a number of provinces to enter into mutual arrangements satisfactory to the dominion government. Unless we can find out what it is that is deterring the provinces, it appears that this will continue to be a cause of frustration. Even after we find out what is the matter, we shall have to find some way to meet the difficulties with which the provinces are confronted.
The next question that seems to have developed before us is that the mortgage companies are hesitant about lending very freely in connection with the building of houses. I can understand why that should be. If taxation continues to grow, as was indicated very well by the hon. member for York West, certainly no prudent organization would risk very much capital in communities where taxation is going to increase as rapidly as it has been increasing. I know that in the community in which I dwell, which is an ordinary small town with about 2,500 of population, the taxation rate has become so great that people simply cannot support the taxation. Nevertheless there does not seem to be anything that the community can avoid. They say: We have got to have schools and we have to have certain other facilities. The demands for these are increasing and we just simply cannot avoid the expense involved. We simply have got to raise the taxation. Those who are charged with responsibility, school boards and other municipal officials, say: Heaven only knows where this thing is going to end. It seems to be getting worse. Therefore we are confronted' with a problem which I presume is general throughout the dominion.
It is not likely that the mortgage companies will be more willing to lend money in future
7, 1951
Supply-Resources and Development than they are now; in fact from the standpoint of ordinary reasoning it would appear that they will become less willing to risk their money. Can the minister see anything we might do to overcome the necessity of having the mortgage companies lend this money? For example, from the standpoint of plain, ordinary common sense I cannot see why in the world we could not use the Bank of Canada to lend money so people would have what they needed, at rates no higher than per cent. Can the minister see any reason why that should not be done? It just seems grotesque, does it not, that a nation like this should be prevented from developing adequate housing for its people simply because the mortgage companies dare not lend the money necessary? It is almost impossible to be reconciled to a situation so unreasonable. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says-the mortgage companies do not want to lend money. I do not blame them. I wager that if the hon. member had at his disposal all the facilities of an ordinary mortgage company, with all the responsibilities that rest upon it, he would not lend money either. What is the use of putting money into houses on which enormous taxation will be imposed, with the danger of losing those houses to the municipalities? Just common sense prudence, which I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is endowed with, would tell him not to do that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If I were head of a mortgage company I would not be the member for Winnipeg North Centre.

That is not answering the question. I have the highest admiration for the hon. member, but we must be realistic in these matters. He speaks as though it were in some manner reprehensible on the part of the mortgage companies that they hesitate to lend money. I do not look upon it in that way at all. The mortgage companies have money in trust, and it is their business to lend money to make money in order to discharge their responsibilities. Certainly no one with any responsibility at all will lend money when there is every chance of not being able to make money, and where in many cases it is likely they will not be able to get the money back, and may lose the whole thing.
This problem must be overcome. I am sure the minister can see there is a problem which amounts almost to complete frustration. 1 should like to know whether he has given any thought to what he can do about it. If he finds that he simply cannot overcome this difficulty let him come in and announce that fact frankly to the house, so hon. members

Supply-Resources and Development may participate freely in a discussion as to the best way out of the difficulty. Surely there is a way out. We have the ability to build houses in Canada. We can produce the necessary goods and materials, and we have the skilled men. I would like the minister to give this question some attention and give the house his reaction. We have two problems. One is the indisposition of the provincial and municipal authorities to participate, and the other is the indisposition of the lending companies to loan the necessary money. That indisposition is completely understandable, and in my opinion no way reprehensible.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Every dollar they loan is guaranteed by the government. They do not lose a cent.
Then how do you account for their indisposition to lend?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Because they want to make more money.

I am quite willing to
undertake an argument with my hon. friends; I have never sidestepped a fight with the socialists in this house, but if the people whose business is lending money to make money are hesitating in doing so, there must be some good reason. Either they cannot make the money, or they have not a reasonably good chance of making it. I do not want to become involved in a lengthy discussion of that aspect of the problem. The simple fact is that if the mortgage companies are unwilling to lend money there is no conceivable reason why we should not use the Bank of Canada to make these loans. That is all there should be to it. If the minister is unwilling to risk using the Bank of Canada there must be something wrong with the minister or with the men who are with him in the cabinet. It is simply idle for us to come here year after year, as we have done since we started grappling with this problem after the war, and wring our silly hands and say this is a problem that cannot be solved. We are 261 men and a fine, effective woman; yet we sit here year after year doing nothing effectively to meet the problem.
I do not say we are not building houses; but it has been recognized quite definitely that we are not building them anywhere quickly enough. The minister and everyone else must recognize that. Well, if we are not building houses quickly enough what is to be done about it? It is not that we do not have the material or the desire on the part of the people. Certainly we have the skill to enable us to build houses, and those are the three determining factors which should govern. We have all the things that are necessary except

the disposition to use the facilities that are at our disposal. If that is not the case let someone prove it. I think I can safely challenge anyone to prove that is not so, as I believe I can challenge anybody to show that we cannot use the Bank of Canada to build houses in Canada.
The next difficulty appears to be that we are running into shortages of material. I will grant that as the danger of war develops we may require more and more construction for military purposes, and we are likely to run out of certain materials. But has the minister canvassed the possibility of using certain kinds of soil in the construction of houses? I understand that this has been done successfully in Germany and other parts of the world. This may sound a bit crude, but when my folks came to Canada, and before that, we were building sod shacks, which were called "soddies". For the first six or seven years of my life I lived in a cabin with a sod roof and with the spaces between the logs of the walls daubed with mud. Let no one imagine I am advocating that we should have people living in log houses with the spaces daubed and the roofs covered with sod, but we would be far better off if thousands of people in this country could have houses even as good as that, and be sure they would not be kicked into the street. But we are not disposed to help them build such shelter; we are disposed to let our people go on suffering. Hundreds of thousands of people in this country today have no assurance that they will have a roof over their heads next year. Sometimes it is because they have children, and people who are renting houses do not want children in them. In most cases the people needing houses simply cannot pay the heavy cost of available housing, houses valued at $8,000 or $9,000. Are these people to be left without housing? Is there any reason why we cannot provide them with some kind of houses?
Now, then, has the minister done anything about probing into the possibilities of using other materials? I think I shall stop now before I have too many questions for the minister to deal with. I shall just summarize those three. The first one is, is there anything we can possibly do to enable the provinces to enter into these agreements? Might I say this, that I think the average provincial government realizes that if the cost of municipal government in the province goes on increasing at the rate it is now doing -and there seems no way of overcoming that increase-then the province simply will never be able to finance the building of the houses necessary within the province. I shall

wager that that is ninety-five per cent of the reason for the provinces hesitating about getting into the housing problem. Now that is the first question.
If that is the case, then obviously it is a financial matter again, is it not? No province has the ability to increase its financial revenues by a dollar, except by the development of industry within that province. It is absolutely limited in the matter of revenue, to its ability to raise money from its people by taxation. It must have assistance from some source, which can resort to other measures, if it is going to be able to enter into the housing business.
The second question concerned the matter of lending money. I should like to have the minister tell us what has been done in respect of securing an alternative to the mortgage company. If nothing has been done, why has it not been done? We are going on year after year doing nothing about it.
The third question is, What has the minister been doing in regard to materials so as to enable us to use soils, if need be, so the people can have houses they can depend upon? Will the minister deal with those three problems?

Mr. Chairman, with respect
to the first question about what we can do to induce the provinces to participate under section 35, I think all I can say is substantially what I said before. We have told them collectively and separately that we would be glad to entertain specific proposals from them. Our legislation is clear. I believe it is understood by the provinces. Again, all I can say is that it is there if they wish to use it.
With respect to the second matter, the availability of mortgage money, in a detailed sense that of course is beyond my scope. It is something I would normally expect the Minister of Finance to deal with. The fact of the matter is that at the present moment the availability of materials for housing, and the availability of mortgage money to build houses, are pretty well in balance. The shortage of mortgage money was going to have an adverse effect on housing, in fact the mortgage companies had just about withdrawn from operations. We felt obliged, in the interests of the Canadian public, to take these steps which we think will keep the housing act alive, even though it means a slightly higher interest rate to the borrower.
When I mention the matter of materials, it brings me to the hon. member's third question as to what we are doing about finding materials that might be suitable for
7. 1951	3837
Supply-Resources and Development housing. The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has a research section which works very closely with the national research council on matters of materials. They are finding substitutes all the time, and approving them for one purpose or another. They are not a matter of great public knowledge, but the fact is that some progress is being made all the time in the matter of new materials	and improved materials for
housing.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the minister's answers. But the minister's answers, all members of the house will agree, amount simply to this. We face complete frustration on each and every one of those three points. There is not anything we can do about removing any one of these three difficulties in our endeavour to provide housing for this nation.
Mr. Chairman, I am prepared to grant that the minister is not to blame for any one of these three problems. But if the members of this house are going to face this thing like grown people, with realism, they have got to do something to help the minister. This is especially true of the members of the Liberal party. If they are going to discharge their responsibility to this nation, they have to do something about it.
Obviously, the facilities are at their disposal if they choose to use them. With respect to materials, the minister said we are conducting research and are making some progress here and there. My question is, why are we not getting the houses? I am sure the member for Spadina was not extreme when he pointed out we are not getting nearly enough houses. But what are we going to do about it? I believe that the discussion we have had this afternoon and tonight has indicated that just about one-third-I would not be surprised if we could say more than that, just about one-half-of the people in Canada simply cannot afford the housing which is being offered under the housing act. Look how serious that is. That means virtually all the people who really need houses cannot get them. Are we not going to do anything about this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Talk about it.
That is right, the Liberals are.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You have been repeating the same thing for the last half hour.
That is just about what the minister has been doing. He certainly has been repeating frustration.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
You have not spoken about debt-free money yet.

Supply-Resources and Development

That is right, and speaking of debt-free money in the presence of some members reminds me of one of the passages in the scripture, "cast not your pearls ..." I ask the Minister of Public Works to get up and tell us what to do about it. It is all very well for him-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You never sit down long enough for me to make a statement.

I have been sitting down. I have not spoken today until now. I have listened nearly all afternoon. At a time when people are simply groaning under the burden of inadequate housing in this country, here we are going to finish this discussion once more apparently with nothing done. That is all there is to it. The interest rate is raised, and the government's aggregate assistance to the people who would build has been cut down.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Write to your friends in the government of Alberta to do their share, and everything will be all right.
The government of Alberta can show the whole Dominion of Canada a mighty fine record-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They are not coming under section 35.

If the hon. member wants to have a discussion on the matter of Alberta I shall give him the opportunity and make him look like two cents. This sort of silly, flippant, idiotic remark about the government of Alberta is just an example of general Liberal irresponsibility. It is irresponsible to make a general statement like that. It is made so the press will pick it up and make it look as if something was said. After all, the something that was said demonstrated that there was "nobody home" in the head of the speaker.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there is one more thing and that is this-I am not repeating nearly as much as the Minister of Public Works would have it appear. The ordinary individual who wants to build himself a home-a modest little home, one that he can afford-today has no facilities whereby he can do so. Throughout this country there are great numbers of people who build their own homes just as men used to build their own sod shacks and their own log houses. They would build their own homes and they would learn how to do the building readily if they could only get a loan and get the material with which to build the homes. To tell us in Canada that materials of the kind are not available is to be absolutely unrealistic; and every member of this committee knows that right well. There

certainly are in this country materials which can be used for building; and the people, generally speaking, would use those materials and build the houses, if they could get the money with which to buy the materials. But we will not let them have the money because we say we have got to get it all from the mortgage companies and that we cannot lend it to them except under certain circumstances. We therefore have to go on facing complete frustration.
I do not propose to say any more about this matter just at the present time, Mr. Chairman. If the people throughout the country could realize and know how many times during the last hour and a half we have had from the Liberals all over the place calls of "carried, carried", and could realize how completely that indicates the utter indisposition on the part of those members to find a solution for the problem, I do not know what they would do. I suppose they would go and. elect a Liberal government right away again, because they would not have any alternative.
Hear, hear.

They would have no
alternative-I suppose I shall be out of order-because the Conservative party which faces them has exactly the same policy as the Liberals have, and the same ideas. There is not the slightest difference in the world.
Say not so.
One does not have to say it. We are listening to it all the time. To say that there is no alternative as far as the Conservatives are concerned is quite obvious, and does not need to be said.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

All right, Mr. Chairman.
I just wish to make this point. If people could realize how fcompletely irresponsible the great, big, overwhelming Liberal party is in this house with respect to this matter of building houses, they would be astounded.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. It appears
to me that the remarks being made by the hon. member are not relevant to the item under discussion.

I oan be relevant, Mr. Chairman, if relevancy is all that is necessary. I can speak right on this matter I am talking about, and I can say plenty more. The great question is this: When the members of the House of Commons go back to their constituencies, they will simply have to tell the people that nothing is to be done for housing.
You take your chance.

Of course you take your
chance. But the question is this: Will you get the houses? That is the thing that counts. Will you give the people that chance to have housing? The answer that is given by the Liberals is: No, we do not need to. Let them suffer. We do not care. We will not suffer. We Liberal members of parliament will be able to have houses. What do we care about the poor fellows down under who are getting too small an income to enable them to get a home? We do not care a button about them. They do not amount to anything at all. That is just the attitude of the ordinary Liberal. That is just exactly his attitude.
Oh, no.
That is the attitude.
Oh, no, it is not.
The general attitude will be this: they will have to take it or leave it; we do not care.
Oh, no, it is not.
Oh, yes, it is.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I shall have to ask the hon. member not to discuss what he considers to be the attitude of other members of the House of Commons. He must discuss housing.

I am certainly discussing housing from the standpoint of about 45 per cent of all the people in Canada who find housing completely beyond their reach. The number of people in every community in this country who are wondering how in the world they are going to be able to afford housing is sufficiently large to constitute a complete scandal in this nation. I refer to the people who are called upon to pay $75, $80 or $90 for an apartment, when the cost of that living apartment likely uses up more than half of their total income. They must have housing. They have no alternative. That is a serious problem.
The point is that up until the present time this parliament has not done anything effective about the matter of housing. It chooses to leave at least forty per cent of the total population of Canada with inadequate housing and to indicate to the country that it is not ready to do a thing about it. No matter what facilities may be available to it with which to do something about it, it refuses to use those facilities. It chooses to let forty per cent of the people go with inadequate housing.
That is all, Mr. Chairman. If that is not enough to fill with shame all the men who
7, 1951
Supply-Resources and Development have responsibility in this parliament, then all I can say is that they just are not qualified to appreciate reality at all.

Following up the discussion we have just heard, may I say that I notice by this report of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that last year the corporation made 476 loans directly for the building of non-farm homes and 3 loans for the building of farm homes. I should like to know just what is the policy of the corporation with regard to the making of direct loans, both urban and rural, and just why it is that there were only three farmers in Canada last year who obtained loans from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The reason there were only three loans to farmers is that there were only three applications.
What is the policy with regard to direct loans? I refer to non-farm loans.
The whole policy underlying direct loans is that they will be made in outlying areas where lending institutions do not normally operate.

Am I led to believe that if farmers made application they would get a loan if everything was found to be correct, and that the only reason that only three farm loans were made is that only three applications were made? Were there not any made, of which some were turned down? It is quite surprising that only three applications were made, and that all three were granted, from all the farmers of Canada. Is that correct?
To the best of my knowledge and to the best of the recollection of the officials of the corporation, that is correct.
Item agreed to.
What item is the chairman calling?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
It was agreed that, instead of item 383, departmental administration, we would discuss the items relating to housing which are items 427 and 565. Item 565 has reference to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Item 427 is the one dealing with emergency shelter administration. Both of those items have been discussed and carried. We will now revert to item 383.
383. Departmental administration, $381,223.

I do not know whether the minister wishes to proceed with this matter tonight. It has been the practice
3840	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Resources and Development
to have a general discussion on the first item, that of administration. The minister's department is an important one, which is asking in the estimates for more than $35 million. There are very many headings.
I do not know of any of them that is as important as the one that was discussed all day and all night, namely, the item of housing.
When the department was organized with the minister in charge we in Nova Scotia and eastern Canada expected a good deal from him and from the department. As one Nova Scotian to another I say to him that I want to see him succeed in his effort and to make a success of his department. But there is a feeling in Nova Scotia that very little progress has been made in the activities that have been assigned to this department.
I have a few items here such as the Chignecto canal and cheaper power for our part of the province. I doubt whether the minister has made an inspection of the Chignecto canal and whether he gave support to its construction when a very large delegation came here. It was rather enlightening to see the interest which the Minister of Transport took in the proposed St. Lawrence seaway. He accompanied a large delegation over the St. Lawrence river inspecting that part of the river in which the seaway is proposed to be built at a cost of hundreds of millions of dollars, and perhaps a billion dollars, which would give cheap power to central Canada when constructed. I do not say that I am opposed to that expenditure, but I would expect some compensating expenditures in my part of the country.
I should like to refer to the St. Mary's tidal power project, which was discussed in this house some sessions ago. The minister gave it his blessing at that time and said that he would see that it was investigated. Ever since that time we have been waiting for a report from the minister. It would create about two million horsepower or more and it would give us cheap power in eastern Canada. While they have cheap power and are looking for still cheaper power in central Canada we have had to meet increased costs of electric power in my part of Canada. The cost of power in that part of the country has increased by as much as one-third, 25 per cent and so on.
During the discussion of his estimates I should like the minister to make a statement on the results of the investigations of the St. Mary's tidal power project at the head of the bay of Fundy. If it could be constructed it would be very important to eastern Canada, and probably would warrant the electric smelting of the enormous tonnage of iron

ore which will be produced in Labrador and which it is expected will be shipped largely to the United States centres.
We have also been disappointed with the progress made in the construction of the bridge over the strait of Canso. While this matter may not come directly under the minister's department, it has to do with resources and development. I presume he is working in close conjunction with the Minister of Transport and the government.
We have also been disappointed in the building and putting into service of the ferry steamship from Nova Scotia to Maine. We have had that promised to us and it has been delayed. Eastern Canada, and especially Nova Scotia, have every reason to be disappointed. There is also the question of the trans-Canada highway which we shall discuss in some detail when the item is called. We were assured that there would be large expenditures long before this in the construction of a trans-Canada highway which would give direct service to every part of Canada by the shortest practical route. In Nova Scotia nothing has been done up to the present. We shall get a further explanation from the minister. Perhaps he will make a general statement on that item when it is called, but anyway we shall expect direct information from him.
In Nova Scotia we have also been disappointed that no headway apparently has been made with the construction of the Blomidon national park. We were given assurance, perhaps not by the minister, but by his predecessor, that headway was being made in building this park.
Another important subject which has to do with resources and development is railway freight rates. I should like to have a general statement from the minister with respect to that as it relates to Nova Scotia. We are not satisfied with the situation there at the present time.
I shall refer to one other item before eleven o'clock, namely, the dispersal of industry and the construction of defence industries in the maritime provinces and the desirability of dispersing these large plants in this country. During the discussion of building houses it was pointed out how difficult it is, in fact almost impossible, to supply housing in the large centres of central Canada to accommodate the workmen required in those centres where as much as $100 million is being expended in a single constituency, which is more than is being expended in all of the maritime provinces under this heading.
As opposed to the dispersal of industry, people from central Canada are going to Nova

Scotia and eastern Canada all the time draining off our workmen. Just a few days ago a large mining concern from central Canada asked for 1,000 men from Nova Scotia, labourers, to supplement the 2,000 that they had already procured in Nova Scotia. That is just one instance. There have been scores of them. Scores of industries are drawing labour from the maritime provinces, and particularly from Nova Scotia, where industries of our own should be established under this heading with the assistance and encouragement of the government.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
